advances: The requested small-score boundary branch is impossible: under the actual minimum-area quantile cores and near-stationarity hypotheses, the score on the shortest reduced-basis vector cannot tend to zero. Thus no sequence satisfies the stronger assumption that both reduced-basis scores tend to zero. This proves the requested weighted boundary conclusion as a consequence of an empty hypothesis class; it does not assert a nonvacuous quantitative boundary estimate or continuous midpoint quadrature. The argument uses one-dimensional integration along the shortest-vector lattice rows, whose error is controlled directly by row endpoint masses, and never assumes the missing two-dimensional weighted boundary estimate.
author: research-agent
external_sources: None. The one-dimensional separation comparison is used only in its proved form inside accepted fact `b09fd2c6d7d7ab1d`; all new chord-integral and rigidity steps are proved above.
proof:
Write \(\mathcal T\) for the exact original-mass-parity canonical operator of `b09fd2c6d7d7ab1d`. Its sampling convention chooses a parity with its original mass and then independent conditional endpoints, not independent original endpoints conditioned globally on matching parity. All occurrences of \(\mathcal T\) below retain that convention. We prove the impossibility assertion by contradiction. Suppose in addition to the stated root hypotheses that \(|\boldsymbol\lambda_k\cdot\mathbf g_{k,1}|\to0\).

Accepted fact `3f23ec160b160e93` gives \(1-\eta_k\le\alpha_k\), completeness of \(F_k\), and \(B(\mathbf0,r)\subseteq\widehat K_k\subseteq B(\mathbf0,R)\), where \(r=1/(3\sqrt2)\) and \(R=2\). Thus \(u_{\max,k}\le p_{\max,k}/(1-\eta_k)\to0\). The conditioning comparison from the global canonical continuity bound in `b09fd2c6d7d7ab1d` gives
\(\operatorname{TV}(u_k,\mathcal T(u_k))\le\delta_k+4(1-\alpha_k)\le\delta_k+4\eta_k\to0\).

Put \(\mathbf v_{k,j}=G_k\mathbf g_{k,j}\), for \(j=1,2\). These two vectors form a unimodular basis of \(\mathbb Z^2\), since the \(\mathbf g_{k,j}\) form a basis of \(G_k^{-1}\mathbb Z^2\). Use integer coordinates
\(\mathbf x=\mathbf u_{k,0}+i\mathbf v_{k,2}+j\mathbf v_{k,1}\).
Then \(A_k\mathbf x=-\mathbf c_\triangle+i\mathbf g_{k,2}+j\mathbf g_{k,1}\). The integer translation and unimodular matrix permute the full original parity classes. Define the signed scores \(a_k=\boldsymbol\theta_k\cdot\mathbf v_{k,2}\) and \(b_k=\boldsymbol\theta_k\cdot\mathbf v_{k,1}=\boldsymbol\lambda_k\cdot\mathbf g_{k,1}\). Thus \(b_k\to0\). There is no assumption or bound on \(a_k\). In these coordinates the conditional law is \(u_k(i,j)=e^{a_ki+b_kj}/L_k\) on the integer points of its coordinate polygon, where \(L_k=\sum_{\mathbf I\in F_k}e^{\boldsymbol\theta_k\cdot(\mathbf I-\mathbf u_{k,0})}=Z_k\alpha_ke^{-\boldsymbol\theta_k\cdot\mathbf u_{k,0}}\).

We first control row endpoints using only the reduced geometry. Suppress \(k\), write \(d_1=\|\mathbf g_1\|\), and put \(h=|\det(\mathbf g_1,\mathbf g_2)|/d_1\). The shortest-vector and nearest-integer reduction in `3f23ec160b160e93` gives \(h\ge\sqrt3d_1/2\). Choose a unit normal \(\mathbf n\) to \(\mathbf g_1\). Lattice rows parallel to \(\mathbf g_1\) have normal coordinates in an arithmetic progression with spacing \(h\), including the affine coset translation \(-\mathbf c_\triangle\).

Let \([s_-,s_+]\) be the normal projection of \(\widehat K\), and let \(\ell(s)\) be its chord length on the line with normal coordinate \(s\). Convexity makes \(\ell\) concave. The ball inclusions give \(s_-\le-r<0<r\le s_+\), \(-s_-\le R\), \(s_+\le R\), and \(\ell(0)\ge2r\). Consequently

\[
\ell(s)\ge\frac{2r}{R}(s_+-s)\quad(0\le s\le s_+),
\qquad
\ell(s)\ge\frac{2r}{R}(s-s_-)\quad(s_-\le s\le0).
\tag{1}
\]

Let \(n_i\) be the number of lattice sites in row \(i\). Completeness makes them a consecutive interval. An interval of Euclidean length at least \((N+1)d_1\) contains at least \(N+1\) points of its affine lattice row. Thus any row meeting \(\widehat K\) and having \(n_i\le N\) has chord length less than \((N+1)d_1\). By (1), its normal coordinate is in one of the two endpoint intervals of length \((N+1)Rd_1/(2r)\). An arithmetic progression of spacing \(h\) meets an interval of length \(T\) in at most \(T/h+1\) points. The number of these short or empty rows is therefore at most
\(2(N+1)R/(\sqrt3r)+2\le12(N+1)\), for every integer \(N\ge0\). In particular there are at most 12 empty rows whose real chords meet the polygon. This estimate includes rows with zero-length chords.

Define the row masses \(R_i=\sum_j u(i,j)\), their largest atom masses \(m_i=\max_j u(i,j)\) on occupied rows, and \(M=\sum_i m_i\). Put \(m_i=0\) on empty rows. In a row with \(n_i\ge N\ge1\), its finite geometric law gives

\[
\frac{m_i}{R_i}
\le\left(\sum_{q=0}^{N-1}e^{-|b|q}\right)^{-1}
\le\frac1N+|b|.
\tag{2}
\]

For \(|b|>0\), the sum is at least \(\int_0^N e^{-|b|x}\,dx=(1-e^{-N|b|})/|b|\), and \(e^{-x}\le1/(1+x)\) proves the last inequality. For \(b=0\) it is immediate. There are at most \(12N\) occupied rows with fewer than \(N\) sites. Summing (2) on the other rows therefore gives
\(M\le1/N+|b|+12Nu_{\max}\).
Choose integers \(N_k\to\infty\) with \(N_ku_{\max,k}\to0\), for example \(N_k=\lfloor u_{\max,k}^{-1/2}\rfloor\) eventually. It follows that \(M_k\to0\).

We next construct a log-concave approximation to the row marginal without a two-dimensional interpolation. In the integer coordinates above, write the real chord at first coordinate \(s\) as \([\ell_-(s),\ell_+(s)]\) in the second coordinate. Define
\(c(s)=e^{as}\int_{\ell_-(s)}^{\ell_+(s)}e^{bx}\,dx\) on the polygon's first-coordinate projection, and zero outside; zero-length chords give value zero. Put \(c_i=c(i)\).

The function \(c\) is log-concave by the following elementary interval calculation. The chord at \((1-t)s_1+ts_2\) contains the Minkowski combination of the two chords at \(s_1,s_2\). For an interval of center \(z\) and length \(q>0\), its exponential integral equals \(e^{bz}H_b(q)\), where \(H_0(q)=q\) and \(H_b(q)=2\sinh(|b|q/2)/|b|\) if \(b\ne0\). The function \(\log H_b\) is concave: its second derivative is \(-1/q^2\) for \(b=0\), and \(-(|b|/2)^2/\sinh^2(|b|q/2)\) otherwise. The centers and lengths of a Minkowski interval combine linearly. Hence its integral is at least the geometric interpolation of the two integrals. Containment of that interval in the middle chord preserves this lower bound, and the factor \(e^{as}\) is log-affine. This proves log-concavity, including zero-length and exterior cases by the zero convention. Thus, whenever normalized, the finite sequence \((c_i)\) is log-concave and has interval support.

Here is a direct error estimate. Put \(H(b)=\int_{-1/2}^{1/2}e^{bx}\,dx\), so \(H(b)\to1\) as \(b\to0\). For an occupied row, let its integer sites be \(j_-\le j\le j_+\), where \(j_-=\lceil\ell_-(i)\rceil\) and \(j_+=\lfloor\ell_+(i)\rfloor\). The integral over \([j_--1/2,j_++1/2]\), multiplied by \(e^{ai}\), is exactly \(H(b)L R_i\). The real chord endpoints satisfy \(j_--1<\ell_-(i)\le j_-\) and \(j_+\le\ell_+(i)<j_++1\). Therefore each endpoint discrepancy between the real chord and the comparison interval has length at most \(1/2\). Every point in the lower discrepancy is at distance less than one from \(j_-\), and every point in the upper discrepancy is at distance less than one from \(j_+\). On either discrepancy, the full integrand \(e^{ai+bx}\) is consequently at most \(e^{|b|}\) times the unnormalized weight of its corresponding occupied endpoint site, and hence at most \(e^{|b|}Lm_i\). The two intervals both contain \([j_-,j_+]\), so their symmetric difference is contained in these two endpoint discrepancies, of total length at most one. Integrating gives
\(|c_i-H(b)LR_i|\le e^{|b|}Lm_i\le2e^{|b|}Lm_i\).

On an empty integer row the chord has coordinate length less than one. The exponential weight anywhere in the entire coordinate polygon is at most \(Lu_{\max}\), because a linear functional attains its maximum at a polygon vertex, and every polygon vertex is a support lattice point. Hence \(c_i\le Lu_{\max}\) on an empty row. There are at most 12 such rows by the previous count. Consequently

\[
\sum_i\left|\frac{c_i}{L}-H(b)R_i\right|
\le2e^{|b|}M+12u_{\max}\longrightarrow0.
\tag{3}
\]

Since \(H(b)\to1\) and \(\sum_iR_i=1\), (3) implies \(\sum_i c_i/L\to1\). In particular \(C_k':=\sum_i c_{k,i}>0\) eventually. Define the auxiliary finite log-concave probability law \(\rho_{k,i}=c_{k,i}/C_k'\). Equation (3) and normalization give \(\sigma_k:=\operatorname{TV}(R_k,\rho_k)\to0\). The symbol \(C_k'\) is only this scalar normalizer and is unrelated to the locked convex body \(C\).

We now compare canonical projection with the one-dimensional canonical map, retaining the full original parity weights. For each row let \(R_{i,c}=\sum_{j\equiv c\pmod2}u(i,j)\), \(c\in\{0,1\}\). A finite geometric row is unimodal. Extend it by zeros; its adjacent total variation is \(2m_i\). Grouping adjacent even and odd entries shows \(|R_{i,0}-R_{i,1}|\le2m_i\). Therefore the probability laws \(\zeta(i,c)=R_{i,c}\) and \(\overline\zeta(i,c)=R_i/2\), on \(\mathbb Z\times\{0,1\}\), satisfy
\(\operatorname{TV}(\zeta,\overline\zeta)=\tfrac12\sum_i|R_{i,0}-R_{i,1}|\le M\).

The first-coordinate projection of \(\mathcal T(\zeta)\) is exactly that of \(\mathcal T(u)\): full parity is \((i\bmod2,c)\), its mass is the sum of \(R_{i,c}\) over the indicated first parity, and the conditional endpoint row law is precisely the same in both constructions. In \(\mathcal T(\overline\zeta)\), the two values of \(c\) instead have equal weights and identical conditional endpoint row distributions. Its projection is thus exactly the one-dimensional canonical law \(\mathcal T_1(R)\), which chooses first-coordinate parity with its original marginal mass. Apply the global 3-Lipschitz total-variation estimate of `b09fd2c6d7d7ab1d` to \(\zeta,\overline\zeta\), and then project. We obtain
\(\operatorname{TV}(R,\mathcal T_1(R))\le\operatorname{TV}(u,\mathcal T(u))+3M\).
The same 3-Lipschitz bound applies in one dimension by the identical two-parity proof, or by embedding a law on \(\mathbb Z\) into \(\mathbb Z\times\{0\}\). Replacing \(R_k\) by \(\rho_k\) therefore gives

\[
\operatorname{TV}(\rho_k,\mathcal T_1(\rho_k))
\le\delta_k+4\eta_k+3M_k+4\sigma_k\longrightarrow0.
\tag{4}
\]

For completeness, we give the needed one-dimensional rigidity argument. The one-dimensional comparison proved in `b09fd2c6d7d7ab1d` establishes, for every finite log-concave interval law \(\rho\),
\(\operatorname{TV}(\rho,\mathcal T_1(\rho))\ge\kappa-3\rho_{\max}\), with precisely that predecessor's constant \(\kappa\). This is its proved comparison between the one-dimensional canonical and globally same-parity-conditioned midpoint operations; we use the canonical side of that comparison. It follows from (4) that eventually \(\rho_{\max,k}\ge m_0:=\kappa/6>0\).

For this compactness argument only, choose a mode \(z_k\) of \(\rho_k\) and define \(\rho_k^\circ(z)=\rho_k(z+z_k)\). Thus \(\rho_k^\circ\) has a mode at zero. Integer translations commute with canonical midpoint formation and only permute its parity classes, so (4) holds for \(\rho_k^\circ\) as well. Put \(J=\lceil2/m_0\rceil\). Monotonicity on each side of a mode and total mass one imply \(\rho_k^\circ(J)\le\rho_k^\circ(0)/2\) and \(\rho_k^\circ(-J)\le\rho_k^\circ(0)/2\): otherwise the \(J+1\) sites on that side through the mode alone have mass greater than \((J+1)m_0/2>1\). If an indicated site is outside the interval support, the same inequality holds with value zero. Log-concavity then implies for every integer \(|z|\ge J\),
\(\rho_k^\circ(z)\le\rho_k^\circ(0)2^{-|z|/J}\le2^{-|z|/J}\).
Indeed, the secant slope of the logarithm beyond \(J\) cannot exceed the slope between zero and \(J\); the argument on the negative side is identical. If \(\rho_k^\circ(\pm J)=0\), interval support leaves no further sites on that side.

These exponential bounds give uniform tightness and a uniform summable bound on second moments. From any subsequence, a diagonal extraction of \(\rho_k^\circ\) gives pointwise convergence to a probability law \(\rho_*\), and tightness upgrades this to total-variation convergence. Its second moment is finite. The canonical Lipschitz proof also holds for countable laws: the same classwise bounds sum absolutely, and midpoint pushforward does not increase total variation. Thus (4), applied to the translated laws, implies \(\mathcal T_1(\rho_*)=\rho_*\).

Use its canonical sampling representation, with conditional independent endpoints \(X,Y\) given parity \(B\), and \(J_*=(X+Y)/2\). Finite second moments give the exact variance decrement
\(\operatorname{Var}(X)-\operatorname{Var}(J_*)=\tfrac12\sum_{c=0}^1\Pr(B=c)\operatorname{Var}(X\mid B=c)\).
Stationarity makes the left side zero. Each occupied parity conditional law is consequently a point mass, so \(\rho_*\) has at most two support sites. Its support is an integer interval: if two sites have positive limiting probabilities, the logarithmic interpolation inequality for the interval laws \(\rho_k^\circ\) gives a positive lower bound at each intervening integer site, and this survives pointwise passage to the limit. Hence its support is one site or two adjacent sites.

The supremum \(\sup_{m\in\mathbb Z}\rho_k(\{m,m+1\})\) is unchanged by the temporary mode translation. It therefore tends to one: otherwise a subsequence with this supremum at most \(1-\varepsilon\) for some \(\varepsilon>0\) would have a translated total-variation limit as above; that limit is supported on two adjacent sites, contradicting that bound. Return now to the original, unshifted \(\rho_k\). Since \(\operatorname{TV}(R_k,\rho_k)=\sigma_k\to0\), choose integers \(m_k\) such that \(R_k(\{m_k,m_k+1\})\to1\).

Return to the original root lattice. The first coordinate \(i\) in our unimodular coordinates is an integer linear functional \(\mathbf w_k\cdot(\mathbf x-\mathbf u_{k,0})\), where \(\mathbf w_k\in\mathbb Z^2\) is primitive: it is the row of the inverse integer basis matrix that takes value one on \(\mathbf v_{k,2}\) and zero on \(\mathbf v_{k,1}\). Therefore the two rows just found lie in a primitive integer slab of width one, with integer offset \(m_k+\mathbf w_k\cdot\mathbf u_{k,0}\). Its original root mass is at least \(\alpha_kR_k(\{m_k,m_k+1\})\to1\). Let \(\varepsilon_k\to0\) be the original root mass outside that slab. The original-root slab bound of `b09fd2c6d7d7ab1d`, with width \(\omega=1\), gives

\[
\delta_k\ge
\frac{[\kappa-6p_{\max,k}/(1-\varepsilon_k)]_+}{5}
-4\varepsilon_k.
\tag{5}
\]

The right side tends to \(\kappa/5>0\), while \(\delta_k\to0\), a contradiction. This proves that the shortest reduced-basis score cannot tend to zero. Every argument used the original root in (5), with the auxiliary core law used only in its explicitly stated conditioning and row comparisons.

Finally, the specified cells use the exact transported coset and the reduced basis. Their area factor is \(v_k\), and cellwise integration gives the displayed formula for \(\beta_k\); the predecessor's diameter bound gives the stipulated fine mesh. The transported parity classes have already been preserved by the exact affine and unimodular coordinate maps. Since both scores tending to zero entails the impossible shortest-score assumption, the stated boundary implication follows. This last implication is vacuous, as asserted, and supplies no unproved comparison between uniform cell offsets and averaged endpoint offsets.
statement:
Use exactly the root laws, quantile cores, maps, and reduced bases of accepted fact `3f23ec160b160e93`, with the root canonical operator and total-variation convention of accepted fact `b09fd2c6d7d7ab1d`. Explicitly, let \(D_k=\operatorname{conv}(D_k)\cap\mathbb Z^2\) be finite and of affine rank two, and let \(p_{k,\mathbf I}=e^{\boldsymbol\theta_k\cdot\mathbf I}/Z_k>0\) on \(D_k\), extended by zero elsewhere. Define

\[
\begin{aligned}
\pi_{k,\mathbf b}&=\sum_{\mathbf I\equiv\mathbf b\pmod2}p_{k,\mathbf I},\\
q^{\mathrm{can}}_{k,\mathbf J}
&=\sum_{\mathbf I:\,\pi_{k,\mathbf I\bmod2}>0}
\frac{p_{k,\mathbf I}p_{k,2\mathbf J-\mathbf I}}{\pi_{k,\mathbf I\bmod2}},\\
p_{\max,k}&=\max_{\mathbf I}p_{k,\mathbf I},
\qquad \delta_k=\frac12\sum_{\mathbf I}|p_{k,\mathbf I}-q^{\mathrm{can}}_{k,\mathbf I}|.
\end{aligned}
\]

Suppose \(p_{\max,k}\to0\) and \(\delta_k\to0\). Put \(\eta_k=\sqrt{p_{\max,k}}\). Choose \(K_k\) to be a minimum-area convex hull of a subset of \(D_k\) carrying original mass at least \(1-\eta_k\), put \(F_k=K_k\cap\mathbb Z^2\), and put \(\alpha_k=p_k(F_k)\). Let \(\mathbf u_{k,0},\mathbf u_{k,1},\mathbf u_{k,2}\) be the maximum-area triangle vertices used in `3f23ec160b160e93`, and set

\[
\begin{aligned}
G_k&=[\mathbf u_{k,1}-\mathbf u_{k,0}\ \ \mathbf u_{k,2}-\mathbf u_{k,0}],
&\mathbf c_\triangle&=(1/3,1/3),\\
A_k(\mathbf x)&=G_k^{-1}(\mathbf x-\mathbf u_{k,0})-\mathbf c_\triangle,
&\Gamma_k&=G_k^{-1}\mathbb Z^2,\\
\widehat K_k&=A_kK_k,
&\boldsymbol\lambda_k&=G_k^T\boldsymbol\theta_k.
\end{aligned}
\]

Choose \(\mathbf g_{k,1}\) shortest nonzero in \(\Gamma_k\), and choose \(\mathbf g_{k,2}\) by the basis extension and nearest-integer reduction in `3f23ec160b160e93`. Then it is impossible that \(|\boldsymbol\lambda_k\cdot\mathbf g_{k,1}|\to0\). In particular, it is impossible that the scores on both these vectors tend to zero.

To specify the requested boundary consequence without altering cosets or parity, let \(u_{k,\mathbf I}=p_{k,\mathbf I}/\alpha_k\) on \(F_k\), extended by zero, and let \(\widetilde u_k(A_k\mathbf I)=u_{k,\mathbf I}\). This is only the auxiliary core-conditioned law; every root-law hypothesis above remains about the original \(p_k\). Its affine lattice is \(-\mathbf c_\triangle+\Gamma_k\), and its original parity classes are exactly
\(G_k^{-1}(\mathbf b-\mathbf u_{k,0})-\mathbf c_\triangle+2\Gamma_k\), for \(\mathbf b\in\{0,1\}^2\).

Take the half-open cell shape \(Q_k=\{s\mathbf g_{k,1}+t\mathbf g_{k,2}:0\le s,t<1\}\) and cell area \(v_k=|\det(\mathbf g_{k,1},\mathbf g_{k,2})|\). The cells \(\mathbf x+Q_k\), for \(\mathbf x\in-\mathbf c_\triangle+\Gamma_k\), partition the plane. Define

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathsf I_k\widetilde u_k(\mathbf y)
&=\sum_{\mathbf x\in-\mathbf c_\triangle+\Gamma_k}
\frac{\widetilde u_k(\mathbf x)}{v_k}\mathbf1_{\mathbf x+Q_k}(\mathbf y),\\
\beta_k&=\int_{\mathbb R^2\setminus\widehat K_k}
\mathsf I_k\widetilde u_k(\mathbf y)\,d\mathbf y
=\sum_{\mathbf I\in F_k}u_{k,\mathbf I}
\frac{\operatorname{area}((A_k\mathbf I+Q_k)\setminus\widehat K_k)}{v_k}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Consequently every sequence satisfying the hypotheses in the assigned boundary test, including both scores tending to zero, satisfies \(\beta_k\to0\), because no such sequence exists. The same logical consequence holds for the stronger sum of the full atom masses of cells that cross the boundary. No continuous midpoint interpolation identity is claimed.
